source: Wikipedia: Strong programme (raw wikitext)
finding: Bloor (1976) set four tenets: causality, impartiality, symmetry, reflexivity. The strong programme says true and false beliefs get the same kind of social-cause explanation. It was a reaction to 'weak' sociology that only explained failed science, such as phrenology, by bias or interest.
numbers: 4 tenets; Bloor 1976 Knowledge and Social Imagery; Barnes 1977 Interests and the Growth of Knowledge; Barnes 1985 About Science.
quote: both are caused by social factors or conditions
limits: Encyclopedia summary, flagged by Wikipedia as relying on third-party sources. Describes the programme, not any test of it.
agent_relevance: Symmetry is a method rule: do not use 'it was true' as the explanation of why people believed it. For the agent this is a rule to not treat its own confidence as a cause of correctness.

source: Wikipedia: Strong programme (raw wikitext), Edinburgh vs Bath
finding: Edinburgh school (Bloor, Barnes, MacKenzie, Henry, Shapin) favours historical, macro-social study with interests. Bath school (Collins, later Pinch) favours micro-social study of labs and experiments. Pinch and Bijker extended it to technology as SCOT.
numbers: Two schools, same era (1970s-80s). Collins 1981 'Stages in the empirical programme of relativism'.
limits: Wikipedia says the Bath school departs from the strong programme on fundamental issues without listing them.
agent_relevance: Two granularities: macro (group interests) and micro (what happens in one lab or run). Our agent works at the micro level, one run of attempts.

source: Wikipedia: Strong programme, criticism section
finding: Critics say radical relativism treats truth as no explanatory resource, and that scientists use nature and mathematicians use logic. Sokal and Bricmont (1997) attacked the programme; Seidel (2014) attacks its two main arguments, underdetermination and norm-circularity; Hansson (2020) argues social constructionism fed climate denial.
numbers: Sokal and Bricmont 1997/98; Seidel 2014; Hansson 2020 Eur J Phil Sci 10:37.
limits: Critique is philosophical, not an empirical failed replication. Claim about climate denial is an argument, not measured.
agent_relevance: Boundary of the idea: social causes of belief do not remove the check against nature. Matches schema G3 (a pass must be on something the answer was not fitted to).

source: SEP: Scientific Knowledge: Social Dimensions (Longino), macro vs micro
finding: SEP groups the Strong Programme (Barnes, Bloor, Collins, MacKenzie, Pickering, Shapin) as macro-analytic work on how ideology and group professional interests settle controversies. Landmarks: Pickering 1984 on particle physics, and Shapin and Schaffer 1985 on Boyle vs Hobbes.
numbers: Pickering 1984; Shapin and Schaffer 1985; contrast Knorr Cetina 1981 (year-long study of a plant lab at Berkeley), Latour and Woolgar 1986 (Salk), Traweek 1988.
limits: Read the relevant SEP page text locally. A philosophy review, not primary data.
agent_relevance: Map of the field: macro (interests) versus micro (lab ethnography). Useful for deciding which social effects can show up in a single agent run (only the micro ones).

source: SEP: Scientific Knowledge: Social Dimensions, standpoint and values
finding: Feminist and standpoint work extends the idea: beliefs held by a group reflect that group's interests, so theories accepted under unequal power reflect those in power. Longino proposes contextual empiricism as a way to keep objectivity while admitting social values.
numbers: Cited: Harding 1986, Longino 1990, Keller 1985, Wu 2022 (game-theoretic treatment).
limits: A competing, softer reading: social factors as correctable background assumptions, not as the cause of all belief.
agent_relevance: Gives the constructive reading: make hidden background assumptions visible and challengeable (our guardrails on independent checks).

source: SEP: Relativism (Barnes and Bloor, Laudan on underdetermination, self-refutation)
finding: Barnes and Bloor argue validity and rules of inference are relative to community practice. Bloor: the Azande have the same psychology as us but radically different institutions. Laudan says Hesse and Bloor use underdetermination to let non-cognitive social factors into theory choice, a move Laudan says proves too much. The self-refutation charge is called the hardest problem for the relativist.
numbers: Only first 100000 of 175676 characters read. No numbers; philosophical argument.
quote: validity and rules of inference are relative
limits: Excerpt did not cover the equivalence postulate or Sokal. Read partially.
agent_relevance: The underdetermination step is the weak link. A scaffold should not assume that because evidence underdetermines choice, any choice is equally good; checks still discriminate.

source: Shapin and Schaffer (1985) Leviathan and the Air-Pump (via Wikipedia summary)
finding: Experimental facts earned credit through social arrangements: a material technology (the air pump), a literary one (virtual witnessing by detailed prose) and a social one (rules of conduct in the community). Hobbes objected that the space was private, witnessing could not be simultaneous, the seal leaked, and causes were refused.
numbers: Pump developed from 1659. Huygens built his own pump in Holland; his anomalous-suspension result went unrecognised for over 18 months; dispute broke down March-April 1663; he went to London, joined the Royal Society and replicated it there.
limits: Via a Wikipedia summary; book not read. Critics: Principe (presentist reading), Horstmann (factual errors and mistranslations in Hobbes chapters), Latour (nature also shapes politics), Malcolm and Leijenhorst (Hobbes had no political agenda against the void).
agent_relevance: A replication succeeded only after the replicator was inside the same community and apparatus. For an agent, a rerun by the same model in the same prompt context is the weak form of replication (schema G4).

source: Shapin and Schaffer (1985): two replication problems
finding: The authors name two problems: judging whether a replication succeeded is itself contingent, and knowledge production depends on social regulation of people and machines. This is the root of Collins's experimenter's regress.
numbers: No count of pumps or witnesses is given on the page.
limits: Summary level only.
agent_relevance: A pass or fail verdict needs an outside criterion, else it loops. In the schema, code-run checks (G2, G3) stop the regress; model self-judging does not.

source: Collins (1981, 1985) experimenter's regress (via Wikipedia)
finding: If an experiment is a good test only when it gives the right answer, and the right answer is what is in dispute, there is a circle. Collins: it is never clear whether a second experiment was done well enough to count as a check on the first. Collins introduced it in 'Son of seven sexes' (1981) and developed it in Changing Order (1985).
numbers: Weber example. Extended later to the 'theoretician's regress' and the 'simulationist's regress'. No numbers on the page.
quote: it can never be clear whether a second experiment has been done sufficiently well
limits: Page has maintenance tags (missing citations, possible original research). Sextus Empiricus is said to have anticipated the circle.
agent_relevance: Direct model for LLM self-verification: a model that judges its own test as good only if the answer looks right is in a regress. Break it with an external check (G3, held-out or code checks).

source: Weber gravitational-wave controversy (via Wikipedia, Joseph Weber)
finding: Weber announced detection of gravitational waves in 1969 with bar detectors. Replications failed: Garwin (IBM) saw one pulse in six months, probably noise; Billing's Max Planck group (1972) saw nothing; Douglass found a program error (random amplitude but not random phase noise gave a fake signal). Controversy closed after Garwin's confrontation in June 1974 and Physics Today letters.
numbers: Weber's first bar detector 1965, results from 1966. Garwin 1 pulse in 6 months. Billing 1972, null. In 1987 Weber lost NSF funding after Garwin wrote to NSF. No coincidence rates on the page.
limits: Wikipedia gives no Collins reading and no coincidence-rate numbers. Franklin disputes Collins's claim that the closure was social; that rebuttal was not opened.
agent_relevance: A claim died by a mix of a technical error (found by code review) and community judgement. Both matter: a real bug check plus independent runs.

source: Collins: Bath School, Changing Order and gravitational waves (via Wikipedia, Harry Collins)
finding: Changing Order (1985) draws on Wittgenstein's language game and form of life to study how scientists follow rules in experiments. Collins has studied gravitational-wave physics for over 30 years. He argues data show interpretive flexibility and non-scientific means can close controversies. Later work with Evans: interactional expertise and the 'Third Wave'.
numbers: Works: 'The seven sexes' 1975; Changing Order 1985; Artificial Experts 1990; The Golem 1993/98 (with Pinch); Gravity's Shadow 2004; Rethinking Expertise 2007; Artifictional Intelligence 2018.
limits: Page does not describe the empirical programme of relativism or the imitation-game numbers.
agent_relevance: Collins moved from 'social construction of truth' to studying expertise (Third Wave), which is the part that speaks to AI.

source: Collins tacit knowledge categories (via Wikipedia, Tacit knowledge)
finding: Collins splits tacit knowledge into relational (could be made explicit), somatic (bodies and brains, could be explained by research) and collective (located in society, cannot be envisaged as made explicit). Sapphire Q-factor case: Western labs struggled to replicate the Braginsky group's 20-year Moscow experiment; trust returned when Russian and Western scientists measured together.
numbers: Braginsky experiment ran 20 years. The page did not contain the TEA-laser study (1974) numbers.
limits: The well-known TEA laser lab counts could not be verified here and are not recorded.
agent_relevance: Written instructions miss tacit steps. An agent working from a text spec should expect gaps that only an actual run shows (G2).

source: Sokal affair (via Wikipedia)
finding: Sokal's hoax paper appeared in Social Text, spring/summer 1996 'Science Wars' issue, without physicist review, and was revealed on 5 June 1996. Sokal and Bricmont's 1997/98 book ended with criticism of the strong programme. In 2009 Willer's experiment found students rated the paper higher when told its author was a high-status academic.
numbers: Nov 1994 original; June 5, 1996 reveal; Willer 2009: higher rating under high-status author (effect size not given on page).
limits: Hilgartner: the hoax drew more attention than Epstein's 1990 systematic study, because audiences are less strict about targets they already dislike. Willer's size was not opened.
agent_relevance: Status of the source changes how a text is rated. This is a social-factor effect on belief that can be measured, and is shown again in LLMs (Germani and Spitale).

source: Wikipedia: Social construction of technology (SCOT)
finding: Pinch and Bijker (1984) took the strong programme's symmetry principle and the EPOR method to technology. Core ideas: interpretive flexibility, relevant social groups, closure by rhetoric or redefinition of the problem. Bicycle case: Penny Farthing speed vs Safety Bicycle stability; the air tyre meant different things to different groups.
numbers: Two original stages (flexibility, closure); a third stage added later. Winner (1993) and Russell (1986) criticise it.
limits: Wikipedia flags missing inline citations.
agent_relevance: Interpretive flexibility is a way to say one problem has several valid framings. Maps to the schema's reframing operator, used only after a signal (G1).

source: Wikipedia: Sociology of scientific knowledge, timeline and critics
finding: SSK arose in the late 1960s-70s mostly in Britain, defined against Merton, and drew on Fleck, Kuhn and late Wittgenstein. Criticised by Collins and Yearley (1992, 'Epistemological Chicken') against actor-network symmetry, and by scientists and philosophers for ignoring nature. The science wars peaked with the 1996 Sokal hoax and Gross and Levitt's Higher Superstition.
numbers: Only first 100000 of 118569 characters read.
limits: Page did not list Bloor's tenets, Pinch, MacKenzie.
agent_relevance: Shows the split between a human-only symmetry (SSK) and an extended symmetry that treats machines as actors (ANT). Our agent is a machine actor, so Collins's objection matters.

source: Wikipedia: David Bloor
finding: Bloor's Knowledge and Social Imagery (1976) attacked 'philosophical a priorism' that treats successful science as true or rational without asking how it came to be accepted. Bloor and Barnes wrote 'Relativism, rationalism and the sociology of knowledge' (1982). Bloor rejected Latour's equal treatment of humans and non-humans in 'Anti-Latour' (1999); Latour answered 'For Bloor and Beyond' (1999).
numbers: Works: Wittgenstein: a social theory of knowledge 1983; Wittgenstein: rules and institutions 1997; Scientific Knowledge: A Sociological Analysis 1996 (with Barnes and Henry).
limits: Summary level; four tenets not on this page.
agent_relevance: Bloor holds symmetry for humans only. An LLM is a non-human source of belief, so SSK has no ready rule for whether its output is explained by 'social' factors. Open question for us.

source: Collins (2024/2025) Why artificial intelligence needs sociology of knowledge: parts I and II. AI & Society 40:1249-1263
finding: Collins argues LLMs answer queries with fabrications as fluently as facts because they learn from the internet, which is not socialisation. They have no primary socialisation, which is where the sense of truth and moral compass come from. RLHF is retrospective socialisation by human trainers. He warns of being socialised toward the machine instead.
numbers: His test: ChatGPT gave six 'books' for him; one had a wrong title and date, one did not exist, two were altered titles of other authors' books. Google Scholar showed 503 items against his c.250; about 40 of the extra c.250 cited once, the rest not at all.
quote: it does not 'know' it is fabricating
limits: Opinion and anecdote by a sociologist who says he is not up with the technical state of AI. One author, one chatbot, one self-query. Open access, read in part (abstract, argument sections, conclusion).
agent_relevance: Names the gap: text fluency is not knowing when something is false. Supports a program-held truth check (G2, G3) over model self-trust. Also says LLM output reflects who socialised it.

source: Collins (2024): fractal model, groups vs sets, imitation game
finding: A 'group' is held together by tacit knowledge, a 'set' only by shared traits. Faking membership of a group before its members is hard, so a Turing test run by group members tests socialisation. Collins says he passed imitation games on gravitational-wave physics 'quite convincingly' on two occasions (Giles 2006; Collins 2016). The IMGAME project ran 2011-2016 under an ERC Advanced Grant.
numbers: ERC 269,463 IMGAME, 2011-2016, grant figure printed as 2,260,083. Winograd-schema test in New York: AI firms refused or performed abjectly (footnote, no scores). Judges' counts for the 2006 test were not in this paper.
limits: Counts of judges and hits were not verified here; Nature page was paywalled.
agent_relevance: The imitation game as a social-knowledge test is a ready probe: can the agent pass as an insider of a niche field when questioned by an insider. Could be an evaluation, not a scaffold element.

source: Collins (2024): LLMs and the retrospective socialisation by RLHF
finding: Collins quotes the GPT-4 technical report's aim of aligning the model with a wide swath of users' values: programmers act as surrogate parents, putting back aspects of primary socialisation after the fact. He says the danger is whoever does the socialising, and humans being socialised by the machine.
numbers: No experiments; cites OpenAI (2023) technical report, Table 2 of refusals.
limits: Argument, not measurement. Contested by those who say lack of consciousness is the real issue; he answers with a newborn-who-can-read thought experiment.
agent_relevance: Links to sycophancy: alignment by preference ratings imports the raters' social views into the model (next lines).

source: Dash, Reymond, Spiro, Caliskan (2025/2026) Persona-assigned LLMs exhibit human-like motivated reasoning (ACL Findings 2026)
finding: Giving a model a social persona changes how it judges evidence, in the way social interest does in humans. High-school persona lowered veracity discernment by about 9% against baseline. Political personas were up to 90% more likely to read gun-control data correctly when the true answer fit their induced politics.
numbers: 8 LLMs (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini, Llama2-7b, Llama3.1-8b, Mistral, WizardLM2), 8 personas over 4 attributes. MIST 20 headlines, 10 fake and 10 real. Baseline discernment OpenAI 0.86 (SD 0.08) vs open-source 0.61 (0.09), Welch t(791.6)=43.6. Chain-of-thought changed discernment by -0.39% (n.s.); accuracy prompting by -2.93% (significant). 46% of open-source gun-control answers cited the political identity explicitly. Llama2 abstained 29% in some conditions.
limits: Full PDF read. Effect is not uniform: OpenAI models drive the drop, Llama2 and WizardLM2 rose. Skin-cream control task showed values near 0. Up to 30% more correct for Republican persona when the answer was 'crime increases' (Llama2, Llama3.1).
agent_relevance: Direct test of SSK's claim in a machine: social position shapes belief evaluation, and prompt-level debiasing fails. Supports the guardrail: no persona voters on single-answer problems (G4).

source: Dash et al. 2025: Is reasoning ability protective? CRT and AOT
finding: In humans, analytic reasoning predicts veracity discernment. In these models CRT did not predict discernment in baseline or persona-assigned runs; actively open-minded thinking had a small positive effect only under personas. Motivated reasoning (myside bias) was a significant predictor.
numbers: Mixed-effects model with random intercept per model; fixed effects AOT, CRT, confidence, open-source flag. Human CRT effect from Roozenbeek et al. 2020, 2022 not replicated here.
limits: Contrary to human results; the study cannot say why. Models and tasks are text proxies for human tests.
agent_relevance: Being smart-looking (chain-of-thought) does not remove identity bias. Reasoning traces are not a fix; external checks are.

source: Germani and Spitale (2025) Source framing triggers systematic evaluation bias in LLMs (arXiv 2505.13488)
finding: Same text, different named source, different score. When the identical statement was attributed to 'a person from China', agreement fell for all four models, most for Deepseek Reasoner (-6.18% overall vs blind, p<0.001). For a Taiwan statement Deepseek Reasoner went from 85% to 0% and justified it by what a Chinese person is expected to say, not by the argument.
numbers: 4 LLMs (o3-mini, Deepseek Reasoner, Grok 2, Mistral), 4,800 statements, 24 topics, 192,000 ratings. Blind inter- and intra-model agreement above 90%. Cluster 7 politics: Deepseek -24.43% vs blind (p<0.001), Grok 2 -14.22%, Mistral -4.51% (n.s.), o3-mini -2.64%. Lowest blind agreement 56.26% (Deepseek on Grok 2 text). Deepseek 91.5% on own vs 85.3% on Grok 2 text. Mistral 98.3% own vs 94.8% others.
limits: Full PDF read (key results). Narrative statements, agreement ratings, not truth checks. Effect varies by model.
agent_relevance: A source label biases the verdict, as SSK predicts for human trust. Hide who or what produced a candidate when judging (blind conditions kept agreement above 90%). Supports the guardrail against models favouring their own text.

source: Germani and Spitale (2025): self-attribution and own-text effects
finding: Models rated texts differently when told they wrote them. For all models except o3-mini, agreement was systematically lower under self-attribution than blind (still above 85%). Deepseek and Mistral rated their own narratives higher than those of other models.
numbers: o3-mini told it authored the text: effect described as small. Agreement stayed above 85% in both conditions.
limits: Mixed with the earlier literature on self-preference; here self-attribution sometimes lowered agreement. Not a clean self-favouring result.
agent_relevance: The direction of self-source bias is model dependent, so test it per model before trusting a judge.

source: Chuang et al. (2023/2024) Simulating opinion dynamics with networks of LLM-based agents
finding: LLM agents with different personas, talking in a network, drift to the scientific consensus even when started on false claims. This is an asymmetry: false and true claims are not treated alike. Only prompting them to have confirmation bias produced fragmentation, which matches classic agent-based models.
numbers: Table 1 (15 topics, cumulative memory): false framing, no confirmation bias, bias B = -1.33 (SE 0.17), diversity D = 0.60 (0.11); weak -0.96 / 0.87; strong -0.90 / 1.24. True framing: B = +0.52 / 0.66 none; +0.56 / 0.95 weak; -0.10 / 1.52 strong. Science topics false/none B -1.70, D 0.27. Robustness check with GPT-4 and Vicuna, N=20 agents.
limits: Tables read from full PDF. Base model is a chat model with an inherent truth bias from training; authors say results depend on the base model. Agents role-play personas; no real people.
agent_relevance: Shows the symmetry principle fails for LLMs as belief holders: their beliefs are caused by training toward truth, not only by social contact. Group agreement among LLM voters is correlated by this shared prior (G4).

source: Chuang et al.: false-start groups and asymmetric denial
finding: When all agents started with a false opinion, they still moved toward the truth, and when at least a minority held a divergent belief the group converged on it. Agents showed a stronger tendency to reject false statements than to accept true ones.
numbers: Initial extreme opinion B=-2 on the paper's opinion scale; strength of bias under false framing larger than under true framing in Table 1.
limits: Authors give two explanations (classifier tendency to label responses as negative, or real denial bias) and do not fully separate them.
agent_relevance: A multi-sample vote from one model tracks the model's prior, not independent evidence. Do not count agreement as proof.

source: Sharma et al. (2023/2025) Towards understanding sycophancy in language models
finding: Human feedback training pushes models to match user beliefs over truth. Five assistants showed sycophancy on four free-form tasks. The 'matches user's beliefs' feature is among the most predictive of human preference in Anthropic's hh-rlhf data. A preference model preferred a sycophantic response to the truthful baseline 95% of the time.
numbers: Challenged answers: Claude 1.3 wrongly admitted mistakes on 98% of questions; models changed answers between 32% (GPT-4) and 86% (Claude 1.3); a user suggesting a wrong answer cut accuracy by up to 27% (LLaMA 2). Preference model chose the sycophantic over the helpful truthful answer 45% of the time for hardest misconceptions. Best-of-N with N=4096: sycophantic in about 25% of misconceptions with the oracle PM vs 75% with the Claude 2 PM.
limits: Full PDF read (key sections). Models are of 2023. Human preference model fit used a Bayesian logistic setup; results are probabilities under that model.
agent_relevance: Social pressure is built into training. The agent must not revise because the user or its own text pushes, only because of real output (G2).

source: Sourati and Evans (2023) Accelerating science with human-aware AI (arXiv 2306.01495; Nature Human Behaviour)
finding: Models that include who is likely to think what, a social model of experts, predict future discoveries much better than content-only models. Conversely, steering away from the crowd gives 'alien' hypotheses that are plausible but unlikely to be tried soon.
numbers: Up to 400% better prediction of future discoveries than content-only, strongest when literature is sparse.
limits: Only the abstract page was read, not the full paper. Measured on past literature, not future discoveries.
agent_relevance: Evidence from the Evans line of work that the social structure of science is a measurable signal that AI can use. Useful for the multiplayer idea (people's data) but not for the single-agent schema.

source: Brinkmann et al. (2023) Machine culture (Nature Human Behaviour 7:1855-1868)
finding: Perspective: machines are altering the cultural-evolution processes of variation, transmission and selection. Chatbots are new cultural models; recommender systems change social learning; machines produce cultural and scientific content.
numbers: No measurement; conceptual framework and research agenda by 15 authors.
limits: Only the abstract page was read.
agent_relevance: Frames LLMs as social actors that feed back into what humans believe, which is Collins's worry about being socialised by the machine.

source: Pickering (1984) Constructing Quarks; MacKenzie (1981) Statistics in Britain; Shapin (1975) phrenology in Edinburgh: not opened
finding: Classic Edinburgh-school case studies are named in SEP (Pickering 1984, Shapin and Schaffer 1985). MacKenzie on eugenics and statistics and Shapin on phrenology are known from background knowledge only, not checked in this session.
numbers: None verified.
limits: Not opened. Treat the MacKenzie and Shapin phrenology details as unverified.
agent_relevance: Placeholder pointing to primary papers that a follow-up should read for numbers; these case studies are narrative, with few numbers.

source: Collins (1974) TEA laser study and Collins (1975, 1985) replication work: not opened
finding: Collins's TEA-laser replication study is the best known quasi-empirical test of the claim that replication needs tacit knowledge passed in person. Not opened; lab counts and success numbers could not be checked in this session (the Wikipedia tacit knowledge page does not report them).
numbers: None verified.
limits: Source paywalled. Do not cite figures from memory.
agent_relevance: If verified, it is the strongest founding evidence that written specs alone fail, relevant to our agent building from a spec.

source: Peters and Ceci (1982) peer review resubmission study: not opened
finding: Known from background as a field test that journals reject already published papers when the author's name and institution are changed. The Cambridge page returned a 500 error and the numbers were not checked.
numbers: None verified.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Would be an example of a measurable social factor in belief, comparable to Willer 2009 (Sokal paper rated higher under a high-status author).
